newsitem.title: UK: Rate fall hits London reinsurance market premiums.
newsitem.headline: Rate fall hits London reinsurance market premiums.

text.p: The value of reinsurance business handled by the London market has slipped because of falling rates and a greater need among insurers to hang on to their premium income, according to an industry survey.

A poll of two thirds of the reinsurance company market by the London International Insurance and Reinsurance Market Association showed their gross premium incomes fell from 866.8 million stg ($1.4 billion) to 814 million pounds when commercial policies were renewed for 1997.
"We are still in a very competitive market and generally rates are falling, " said Brian Cragg, general manager of Cologne Re Ltd as he presented the surveys findings on Tuesday.
"Most insurers and reinsurers are reporting large profits, but generally the terms they are writing on are getting worse," he said.
Cragg suggested that reinsurance companies, with profits bolstered recently by fewer claims, will start refusing to write business as low rates in order to avoid being hit in the future.

"Some reinsurers are willing to see a reduction in their incomes as they feel that rates are at or below sustainable levels. Until that happens, there will be no change in the competitive situation," he said.

Cragg said the figures also highlighted that the use of proportional reinsurance is disappearing. He said primary insurers are struggling to get as much growth as they would like and want higher premium retention. They are therefore switching to non-proportional treaties which involve less expenditure up front, he said.

The survey suggested there may be fewer contracts being written in the London market - the total having fallen from 19,439 to 17,120. Cragg said this might result from recent consolidation among insurers companies leading to fewer companies passing on larger contracts.

In long non proportional casualty business, 48 percent of rates on lines had decreased and 21 percent remained the same as the previous year. This compared with 24 percent and 33 per cent respectively. The number of contracts fell from 3354 last year to 2837 in 1997, with gross premium income falling from 232.4 million pounds to 225 million pounds.

In short tail non proportional casualty business 64 percent of rates fell and nine percent remained the same, compared with 57 percent and 25 percent respectively in 1996. Contracts written fell from 200 to 171, and gross premium income fell from 11 million pounds to 3.5 million.

In property non proportional property reinsurance, 85 percent of rates fell and only three percent stayed at last years levels, compared to 70 percent and 14 percent respectively in 1996. Contracts written fell from 8882 in 1996 to 7933, and gross written premiums fell from 246.1 stg to 224.1 in 1997.
The figures gave no indication that the use of alternative risk transfer devices such as derivatives and bonds, has impacted the traditional reinsurance markets.
"With reinsurance rates as low as they are there is I no real financial incentive to look to other options," Cragg said. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
